cf.title: Fix write skew under SERIALIZABLE for Tid Scan & Tid Range Scan

input.subject: Write skew observed under serializable isolation

verdict_reasoning: The TID range scan fix (v5-0001) follows the existing seqscan rule and no surviving objection is against it. The TID scan fix (v5-0002) brings back the relation-level locks that cb5b28613d5 removed, and message #14 does not say why a narrower lock is not enough (prior-attempts-1). The entry targets stable branches without saying whether that includes v5-0002 (maintenance-fit-2). Confidence is medium because the v5 patches and their commit messages were not shown.

brief.title: Take relation-level SIREAD locks in TID scans and TID range scans
brief.problem: Under SERIALIZABLE, a TID range scan takes no predicate lock, so two transactions that read the same ctid range and then write can both commit (write skew). A TID scan that probes an empty TID also takes no lock, so a concurrent insert at that TID creates no rw-conflict. Users who rely on SERIALIZABLE get results that match no serial order.
brief.proposed_design: heap_beginscan() acquires a relation-level predicate lock for TID range scans, as it already does for seqscans and sample scans. A second patch does the same for TID scans. The patches add a note to the SO_TYPE definitions and update README-SSI.
user_visible_surface: More serialization failures for SERIALIZABLE transactions that use TID scans or TID range scans, including UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF according to a reviewer.
New isolation test predicate-tidrangescan, plus tests for inserts into an empty table, bitmap scans and TID scans.
author_claims: The bug exists in all branches since TID range scans arrived in Postgres 14; target is stable branches.
Page-level locks are not enough: heap_insert() checks only relation-level locks, and a range can extend past the current end of the relation.
A relation lock is the correct fix with minimum overhead; narrower locking can come as a separate patch.
SERIALIZABLE allows false positives by design, so extra aborts are acceptable.
brief.thread_state: Andrey Borodin finds the TID range scan change correct, and Andres Freund asked for the SO_TYPE note and bitmap scan tests, now added. Matthias van de Meent and Zsolt Parragi object to relation-level locks, and Zsolt cites cb5b28613d5, which added SO_TYPE_TIDSCAN to avoid exactly such locks.
unclear: The latest commit message, v5-0002 content and README-SSI changes are not shown; only v1 prose is available.
No measurement of extra serialization failures or lock overhead for TID scan workloads.
Whether v5-0002 locks the relation for every TID scan or only for probes that find no tuple.
Whether the TID scan fix, which partly reverts cb5b28613d5, is meant for back-patching too.
How the patch handles UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF, which Zsolt says now causes false-positive aborts.

objections.title: TID scan relation lock reverses cb5b28613d5 without addressing its reason
objections.failure_scenario: An application runs a SERIALIZABLE cursor loop with UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF on a table that other sessions write to. After a minor upgrade with v5-0002, each loop takes a relation-level SIREAD lock, so any concurrent write to that table can abort it. The application then sees new serialization failures with no change on its side.
objections.argument: Message #13 reports that cb5b28613d5 added SO_TYPE_TIDSCAN in 2020 to avoid relation-level locks for TID scans, and v5-0002 brings those locks back. Message #14 cites false positives being allowed by design, but does not say why the reasoning of that commit was wrong. The bug in message #11 needs a lock only when a probe finds no tuple, while v5-0002 locks the relation for every TID scan. The CF entry targets stable branches, so the extra aborts would arrive in minor releases.
objections.author_must_show: Why does v5-0002 lock the relation for TID probes that find a visible tuple, and for WHERE CURRENT OF, when cb5b28613d5 deliberately avoided that?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 confirms the relation lock for WHERE CURRENT OF and the conflict with cb5b28613d5, and message #14 answers neither point specifically. The material confirms only the WHERE CURRENT OF case, so "every TID scan" should be stated as likely.

objections.title: Back-patching a contested TID scan change adds aborts in minor releases
objections.failure_scenario: A site on Postgres 14 to 19 applies a minor update. Its SERIALIZABLE workload, which uses ctid lookups or cursor updates, starts to fail with serialization errors at a higher rate. Nothing in the release notes points the site to the cause, so it finds out from application retries and errors.
objections.argument: The CommitFest entry targets stable branches, and both v5 patches sit in one entry. v5-0001 for TID range scans has support in message #7, but v5-0002 is disputed in message #13 and partly undoes an earlier deliberate design choice. Changing locking behaviour that affects ordinary cursor loops is a larger change than the range-scan gap, and the proposal does not separate the two for back-patching.
objections.author_must_show: Is v5-0002 meant for stable branches, and if so, what evidence shows that the added serialization failures are acceptable in a minor release?

critic.reasoning: The CommitFest entry targets stable branches and holds both patches, and no message says whether the disputed v5-0002 is meant for back-patching. The release notes detail is speculative, but the request to state the back-patch scope of each patch stands.

refuted.title: Back-patched TID scan relation lock adds aborts to WHERE CURRENT OF loops
refuted.failure_scenario: An application runs a SERIALIZABLE cursor loop that does UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF on a busy table. After a minor upgrade, each Tid Scan takes a relation SIREAD lock. Any concurrent serializable write to the table then becomes an rw-conflict, and the loop sees new serialization failures in production with no change on its side.
refuted.argument: Message #13 reports that v5-0002 locks the whole relation for UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF, and says a narrower condition could fix this. Message #14 answers that false positives are allowed by design, but that does not explain a jump in abort rate inside a minor release. The TID scan part also partly reverts cb5b28613d5, which existed to avoid these locks. The anomaly in message #11 needs only probes that find no tuple, so locking every Tid Scan in stable branches goes further than the bug requires.
refuted.author_must_show: Can v5-0002 lock the relation only when a TID probe finds no tuple, so WHERE CURRENT OF and successful fetches keep tuple locks in back branches?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 for the lock scope and of maintenance-fit-2 for the back-patch question. It uses the same scenario and the same requested change.

refuted.title: Relation lock on every TID scan reverses cb5b28613d5 without measurement
refuted.failure_scenario: An application under SERIALIZABLE runs a cursor loop with UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF, or updates rows by ctid in batches. After v5-0002, each statement takes a relation SIREAD lock. A concurrent writer to any other row of the table now causes serialization failures that did not occur before, and the users see the new aborts in production.
refuted.argument: Message #13 reports that cb5b28613d5 added SO_TYPE_TIDSCAN specifically so TID scans would not lock the whole relation, and that v5-0002 now locks it for WHERE CURRENT OF. The gap from message #11 only concerns probes that find no tuple, but per the brief v5-0002 may lock for every TID scan. Message #14 answers that false positives are allowed by design. That reply does not explain why visible-tuple fetches, already covered by PredicateLockTID, should pay the cost, and no abort-rate numbers are shown.
refuted.author_must_show: Can v5-0002 take the relation lock only when a TID probe finds no tuple, and leave WHERE CURRENT OF and successful fetches at tuple-level locks?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. It uses the same messages and the same cursor loop scenario, and asks for the same narrower lock condition.

refuted.title: TID scan fix makes common TID scan users pay for a rare case
refuted.failure_scenario: An application under SERIALIZABLE runs a cursor loop with UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF, or updates rows by ctid. After a minor-release update, each such transaction holds a relation-level SIREAD lock and conflicts with every concurrent writer on the table. The application sees new serialization failures and finds out only from its retry rate in production.
refuted.argument: The v5-0002 anomaly needs a TID scan that probes a TID with no tuple, followed by a concurrent insert at exactly that TID (message #11). Few applications do this. Every TID scan under SERIALIZABLE would pay, including WHERE CURRENT OF (message #13), and an earlier commit added SO_TYPE_TIDSCAN to avoid this lock. The author answers that false positives are allowed by design (message #14). That covers correctness, but it does not weigh a back-patched rise in aborts against so narrow a gain.
refuted.author_must_show: Which real workloads probe empty TIDs under SERIALIZABLE, and how much do serialization failures rise for cursor and ctid-update workloads with v5-0002 applied?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 on the cost to TID scans that find a tuple. The claim that few applications probe empty TIDs has no support in the material, and a SERIALIZABLE anomaly is a correctness bug that needs no demand evidence.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The entry targets stable branches, so new serialization failures for TID scans and WHERE CURRENT OF would arrive in minor releases.

performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: v5-0002 takes a relation-level SIREAD lock for TID scans under SERIALIZABLE, which raises the abort rate for cursor loops and ctid updates.

questions: Does v5-0002 take the relation lock for every TID scan, or only when a TID probe finds no tuple?
Why is a lock taken only for probes that find no tuple not enough, given that cb5b28613d5 added SO_TYPE_TIDSCAN to avoid relation-level locks?
Is v5-0002 meant for stable branches, or only v5-0001?
How much do serialization failures rise for a SERIALIZABLE cursor loop with UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF on a concurrently written table with v5-0002 applied?
Can v5-0001 be committed and back-patched alone while the TID scan lock scope is still under discussion?

committability.owner_note: Andres Freund asked for the SO_TYPE note and the bitmap scan tests, and both were added. The owner needs to know SSI predicate locking and the heap scan flags, and nobody has yet settled the lock scope dispute on v5-0002.
committability.liability: The owner signs for changed abort behaviour under SERIALIZABLE in every branch since Postgres 14, and for the partial reversal of cb5b28613d5 if v5-0002 goes in as is.
committability.author_follow_up: The authors posted five versions, added the requested note and tests, and replied to the objection in message #14. A second author joined in September.

priority.reason: The bug is a reproducible SERIALIZABLE anomaly, and the change is small and limited to heapam.c plus isolation tests. v5-0001 looks ready for a committer, but the lock scope of v5-0002 and its back-patch status need agreement first.

provisional_note: The v5 patches, their commit messages and the README-SSI changes were not shown, so the exact lock condition in v5-0002 is taken from messages #13 and #14. Whether a lock taken only for probes that find no tuple closes the gap in message #11 cannot be judged without the code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in Gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adding explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method for serializable isolation, placing page-level predicate locks on entry tree and posting tree leaf pages and copying locks on page splits. It also handled conflict detection when fast update is enabled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewer Alexander Korotkov found the locking scheme redundant and asked for changes: lock posting tree leaves instead of entry tree leaves, apply page-level locks only when fast update is off, add in-code comments, and improve the isolation tests so they actually create posting trees. After his last review the thread had no updates for almost two months, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adds explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method so that serializable transactions detect rw-conflicts at page level. When fast update is on, the patch falls back to coarser locking.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund closed the entry as a duplicate of an older commitfest entry (1466), so it was not rejected on technical grounds. Before that, Michael Paquier had marked it returned with feedback after about two months with no update. Alexander Korotkov's review asked for consistent fast-update conditions, code comments, and isolation tests that build a posting tree.

precedents_retrieved.title: support tid range scan in parallel
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a Parallel Tid Range Scan so that queries with lower and upper ctid bounds can use parallel workers. Parallel block allocation is changed to obey the start block and block limit that heap_setscanlimits() sets.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No visible message rejects the design. Junwang Zhao and Rafia Sabih posted review comments on v4 in August 2024, about a stray blank line, wrong function names in comments, field order and naming, and a missing comment on the changed block-limit check. The visible messages show no reply from the author or new patch version before the entry was returned with feedback in October 2024. Earlier correctness problems that David Rowley found had been fixed in v3.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in SP-Gist index
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds explicit predicate locking to the SP-GiST index access method for serializable isolation. It takes predicate locks only on leaf pages and copies a lock from the original page to the new page during a page split.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Alexander Korotkov found that locking only leaf pages misses conflicts. When choose returns spgAddNode, the insert adds a new branch that earlier scans could have used, so internal pages need predicate locks too. He also found that the patch moves predicate locks only when doPickSplit() allocates a new leaf page, but SP-GiST can move items to free space on another busy page. Daniel Gustafsson returned the patch based on this review.

precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
And this new branch could probably be used by scans we
made in the past.  Therefore, you need to do predicate locking for internal
pages too in order to detect all the possible conflicts.

precedents_retrieved.title: Tid range scan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch teaches TID scans to handle range quals on ctid (>, >=, <, <=, BETWEEN) so that only the matching block range is read, and adds ctid ordering and selectivity estimates. Later versions add a table AM callback to limit the scan range, so that the planner offers TID range scans only for table AMs that support it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The selectivity estimate patches went into PG12, but the range scan part stalled after the table AM API arrived. Andres Freund asked for range handling to move into the heap scan code, since an AM callback based on block limits does nothing useful for AMs like zedstore. The author could not rewrite heapgettup_pagemode that way, asked for help or shelving, and no new patch came within two months.

precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I have had a lot of difficulty making the changes to heapam.c and I think it's becoming obvious I won't get them done by myself.

precedents_retrieved.title: SERIALIZABLE on standby servers
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch allows SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE transactions on standby servers by having the primary write snapshot safety information into commit records and separate WAL records. The standby waits for a point in the WAL stream where a snapshot is known to be safe, using hypothetical transactions that the primary tracks as stand-ins for standby transactions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author called the patch prototype/WIP code with unsolved problems. Two of them are a race between the safety decision and the order of commit records in WAL, and the absence of snapshot safety information in checkpoints. A third is that the primary makes transactions visible in ProcArrayEndTransaction() order while the standby uses commit record order, which can allow serialization anomalies. No review of the general approach came, and the entry was later withdrawn; the visible messages do not show who withdrew it.
matched_queries: serializable tid range scan predicate lock
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And that's precisely the issue: on the primary, transactions become visible to other transactions in the order in which they perform ProcArrayEndTransaction(), but on the standby, they become visible in the order in which they RecordTransactionCommit().

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent matches this idea. [P8] is about narrowing locks for index-only scans and [P4] about SP-GiST predicate locking, and neither recorded reason applies against this proposal. The relation lock for TID range scans (v5-0001) is answered in message #5, so the only objection concerns v5-0002.
The TID range scan fix (v5-0001) follows the existing rule for seqscans and sample scans and adds no syntax, GUC, catalog or dump change. I have no standards or compatibility objection to it.

The proposal changes only which in-memory SIREAD locks heap_beginscan() takes, and it reuses the existing relation-level lock that seqscans and sample scans already take. It adds no WAL record, catalog, on-disk format, wire protocol message or changed struct, and prepared transactions keep their locks through the existing 2PC path. A standby does not run SERIALIZABLE transactions, so replay is unaffected. Back-patching changes only abort behaviour, and other angles cover that.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes which SIREAD locks a serializable transaction takes during TID scans and TID range scans, and adds no new object, privilege, setting or visible information. The extra false-positive aborts are a desirability and design question for other angles. A user with only SELECT can already force relation-level SIREAD locks and similar aborts through a seqscan, so the change gives no new way to disturb other sessions. A relation lock replaces many finer locks, so it does not grow predicate lock memory.
The TID range scan fix (v5-0001) follows the existing seqscan rule in heap_beginscan(), and I have no maintenance objection to it. The page-lock alternative was answered in message #5.

This is a correctness bug fix inside core SSI predicate locking. No existing feature, setting, extension or external tool gives TID scans and TID range scans the missing conflict-in edge. The patch extends the existing heap_beginscan() relation-lock mechanism and adds no second one.

The TID range scan fix (v5-0001) has no demand problem. It fixes a reproducible SERIALIZABLE anomaly in a released feature, and its cost falls only on transactions that use TID range scans under SERIALIZABLE.
